---
title: "Separation, blankets, and boundaries"
---

## Directed and undirected separation {#sec-separation}

Glasso returns an **undirected** graph. Growing a gene panel by
neighbours is therefore not the same operation as blocking paths on a
DAG.

On a DAG, **$d$-separation** uses the direction of edges. A chain is
blocked by conditioning on the middle node; a collider is opened by
conditioning on the collision node (or on one of its descendants). On
an undirected graph, **$u$-separation** ignores direction: a path is
blocked when it meets the conditioning set. @fig-separation draws both.

![Directed $d$-separation (chain blocked, collider opened), undirected
$u$-separation on a minimal I-map, and the nesting of a Markov boundary
inside a Markov blanket.](images/markov_boundary_versus_d_separation.png){#fig-separation}

## Blanket versus boundary

A **Markov blanket** of a variable $X$ is any set $S$ that renders $X$
conditionally independent of the remaining variables
[@pearlProbabilisticReasoningIntelligent1988]. The neighbours of $X$ in
*some* undirected graph that is an I-map are always a blanket, but that
graph may contain redundant edges, so the neighbour set need not be
minimal.

A **Markov boundary** is a **minimal** Markov blanket. For a positive
distribution, that boundary is unique and equals the neighbour set of
$X$ in the **minimal undirected I-map**
[@pearlProbabilisticReasoningIntelligent1988;
@kollerProbabilisticGraphicalModels2009]. The boundary is therefore the
lower bound on the size of a blanket: every blanket contains a
boundary, and the boundary is the smallest one (@fig-separation, panel
C).

In this book, Markov-boundary expansion of marker seeds
(@sec-fs-perspective) means the neighbour set of a fitted undirected
GGM, under the extra assumption that the fitted graph is treated as a
minimal I-map. It does **not** mean $d$-separation on a regulatory DAG.
